questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Mediator pattern?

options.text: Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, so they don't reference each other directly
Access a collection's elements sequentially
Capture and restore an object's state
Ensure a class has one instance

questions.explanation: Mediator centralizes interaction between colleagues. Sequential access = Iterator; capture/restore = Memento; one instance = Singleton.

questions.prompt: How does Mediator change the shape of communication among many objects?

options.text: It replaces a web of many-to-many references with a hub-and-spoke through the mediator
It removes all communication between objects
It forces every object to be a singleton
It makes each object reference every other object

questions.explanation: Colleagues each hold one link (to the mediator), turning a tangled web into spokes around a hub.

questions.prompt: How does Mediator differ from Observer?

options.text: Observer is one-to-many notification to subscribers; Mediator coordinates many-to-many interaction and often holds the interaction logic
They are identical
Mediator only works with one object
Observer converts interfaces

questions.explanation: Observer broadcasts to interested subscribers; Mediator encapsulates the rules of how a set of colleagues interact.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of the Mediator pattern?

options.text: The mediator can become a god object that absorbs all coordination logic
It always causes memory leaks
It makes objects impossible to test
It requires multiple inheritance

questions.explanation: Centralizing all interaction logic can bloat the mediator; the complexity is centralized, not removed.

questions.prompt: Which real-world role is a classic Mediator analogy?

options.text: An air-traffic controller that coordinates planes so they don't negotiate directly
A library lending one shared book
A travel power adapter
A cookie cutter

questions.explanation: Pilots talk only to the tower, which coordinates them — a hub replacing a web of direct deals.

options.text: When only two objects interact and could talk directly
When many interdependent form controls must coordinate
When you want to change interaction logic in one place
When objects should not reference each other

questions.explanation: Mediator earns its keep with genuinely many-to-many coordination; for two objects it just adds a needless hub.
